When SSDP discovery doesn\'t find the camera (camera AP blocks multicast, or the body skips UPnP), enter its IP (and port if not the default 8080). Pulsar probes /ccapi directly — the same URL that loads in your browser.

Enter the camera\'s IP or host[:port].
Couldn\'t reach the camera. Check Wi-Fi and credentials.
Sub-second exposures can\'t be timed reliably over the camera connection. Set the shutter speed on the camera (Timelapse mode) or use the ESP32 transport for precise short exposures.
Camera autofocuses before each shot. Best for daylight subjects.
Camera shoots at the current focus position. Best for astro / star fields (AF would hunt on stars and drift).
Couldn\'t start live view. Make sure the camera isn\'t in Bulb mode on the body (live view is disabled there) and that no other app is connected.
Set the lens to AF mode on the body switch — drive focus only works with the motor engaged. Once you\'re happy, you can flip the lens to MF to lock the position.
Before we can drive focus and stream live view, the camera needs to be set up. Once done, tap Next.
Set the lens AF/MF switch to AF (if your lens has one). Drive-focus only works when the motor is engaged.
Set the camera mode dial to M. Live view is disabled while the body is in Bulb — focus first, then switch the dial to B for your astro run.
Point the camera at a bright star (or a distant point light source) — the brighter the star, the more responsive the sharpness readout.
Tap a bright star in the image below. A yellow circle will lock onto it. Pulsar measures the peak brightness in that circle as you focus.
Focus is set. To make sure nothing shifts during your astro run:
If your lens has an AF/MF switch, flip it to MF now. This physically disconnects the focus motor — bulletproof.
If your lens has no AF/MF switch, leave it. Pulsar sends \"AF off\" with every bulb shot anyway (the per-shot toggle in the wizards), so the motor won\'t move during the run.
Don\'t touch the focus ring. On most modern lenses the ring is electronic and will move focus even in MF.
Pulsar needs CCAPI active on your camera. Most R-series bodies need a one-time activation:
1. Download Canon\'s CCAPI Activation Tool from the developer portal.
2. Plug the camera into a PC via USB, run the tool, and follow its prompts.
3. On the camera, open Menu → Communication → Wi-Fi settings.
4. Select Camera Control API and create / join a network (camera AP or your LAN).
5. Make sure your phone is on the same network, then re-run the scan.
For multi-hour astro runs, set the camera\'s Auto power off to Disabled (Menu → Setup) so it doesn\'t nap during the gap between shots.
Battery: CCAPI + WiFi roughly halves a normal battery life. Plan ~2 h per LP-E17 on the RP; for longer runs use USB-C power passthrough (DR-E18 coupler).
Set camera to BULB — Pulsar controls exposure

Fires a single shot via the camera\'s smartphone shutter. The camera owns the exposure (its own shutter-speed setting) — Pulsar just sends a press-and-release event.\n\nFor long exposures (Bulb), use Manual instead.
Intervals under 4 s aren\'t recommended — the camera needs time to recover and write each shot to the card.

The connection to your camera dropped during the session, so shooting stopped. Check the camera — if it was mid-exposure (Bulb), it may still be exposing; press the shutter or power-cycle it to be safe. Then reconnect and restart the run.

Automate complex timelapse sequences or burst captures with precision timing.

• Set your camera to Bulb mode so Pulsar controls the shutter.
• Interval is the gap between exposures — the wait time after one shot before the next fires.
• Exposure is how long the shutter stays open per shot.
• Cycle time per frame = exposure + interval.
• Start Delay gives you time to step away before the sequence begins.
• The Sequence Estimate card shows total duration and end time.
Power the Pulsar trigger and check the status LED is blinking.
Keep your phone within a few meters and Bluetooth enabled.
Pull down to refresh — your device will appear above.
No runs recorded yet. Start a sequence and it will appear here.
All recorded runs will be removed. This cannot be undone.

Direct manual shutter control with two modes.

• HOLD: The shutter stays open as long as you press the button. Release to close. Ideal for quick bulb shots.
• LOCK: Tap once to open the shutter, tap again to close. Best for long exposures where you don’t want to hold the button.

Switch between Hold and Lock using the segmented buttons in the action area.
Toggle behaviour using the chips in the action area below.
LOCK: Tap the center button once to open the shutter, tap again to close. Best for long bulb exposures.
HOLD: Shutter remains open as long as the center button is pressed. Ideal for quick bursts.

Calculate the longest exposure that keeps stars as sharp points instead of trails.

• Choose your sensor preset (crop factor) and lens focal length.
• 500 Rule: classic formula, generous — some trailing on modern sensors.
• 400 Rule: tighter, better for high-resolution sensors.
• NPF Rule: most accurate — uses pixel pitch and f/2.8 aperture for sharp stars.
• Formula: Rule ÷ (focal length × crop factor) = max seconds.
• Gap is the pause between exposures for the camera to write to card.
• Adjust shot count and delay just like in Intervalometer mode.
ⓘ This is an estimation — tap for details

The NPF rule calculates: (35 × aperture + 30 × pixel pitch) ÷ (focal length × crop factor).

Since Pulsar doesn't know your camera's exact sensor specs, we estimate based on your crop factor:

• Pixel pitch: %1$s μm (typical for ~24 MP sensors of this format)
• Aperture: f/%2$s (common for astro lenses)

These assumptions work well for most modern cameras. For higher-resolution sensors (e.g. 45–61 MP full frame), the actual pixel pitch is smaller, meaning this estimate is slightly generous — you may see minor trailing.

For exact results, use an online NPF calculator with your specific camera and lens specs, then enter the computed exposure manually in Intervalometer mode.

Configure the ESP32 GPIO pins connected to your shutter and focus optocouplers.

• Only safe output-capable pins are listed.
• Changes are sent to the device immediately and persisted in flash.
• The shutter and focus pins must be different.
• Not available in simulator mode.
GPIO configuration not available in simulator mode
Long astro runs with the screen off can be throttled by Android\'s Doze mode. Allowing background activity keeps Pulsar polling cleanly until the run finishes.
Doze can pause BLE notifications and CCAPI polling when the screen is off for long stretches.

Save and restore all your Pulsar settings.

• Export creates a JSON file with all preferences, defaults, GPIO config, and planner data.
• Import loads settings from a previously exported file.
• Use this to transfer your setup to a new phone or as a safety backup.

Plan and track astrophotography sessions across multiple locations and dates.

• Create events with date ranges (e.g. a star party weekend)
• Add sessions with GPS coordinates, dates, and time windows
• Automatic weather and sky condition checks per session
• Share events as .pulsar files or calendar entries (.ics)
• Import shared events from other Pulsar users

Control how often weather and sky-condition data is refreshed.

• Dashboard data (weather, moon phase, cloud cover) is cached locally.
• A shorter interval gives fresher data but uses more API calls.
• 24 h is a good balance for most sessions planned a day ahead.

Use your phone's sensors to polar-align a star tracker mount.

• Shows real-time azimuth and altitude readings
• Target Polaris (Northern hemisphere) or Sigma Octantis (Southern)
• Calibrate by placing the phone flat and pressing calibrate
• Fine-tune with the altitude and azimuth adjustment knobs on your mount

For best accuracy, keep the phone away from magnetic interference.
Dark frames are taken with the lens cap on. They capture sensor noise at the same exposure and temperature as your light frames, enabling stacking software to subtract fixed-pattern noise.
Exposure ramp (Holy Grail timelapse) smoothly transitions from a short to a long exposure over multiple steps. Ideal for day-to-night or night-to-day transitions.

Shows deep-sky objects (nebulae, galaxies, clusters) that are currently above the horizon at your location.

• Objects are sorted by altitude — higher = better positioned
• Green icon: well-placed (above 30°), ideal for imaging
• Grey icon: low in the sky (10–30°), possible but less ideal
• Best results when used during astronomical darkness

This catalog includes ~27 popular astrophotography targets.

Pulsar Trigger turns your phone into a powerful camera controller with four independent ways to reach the camera:

• Pulsar BLE — pairs with the Pulsar ESP32 hardware module wired to your camera's shutter port. Works with any camera that has a remote-release jack.
• Wi-Fi (CCAPI) — drives Canon EOS R-series bodies directly over their built-in Wi-Fi API. No extra hardware.
• USB-C (PTP) — drives Canon bodies (and most PTP-capable cameras) directly over a USB-C cable from your phone. The only phone-side path for the Canon EOS R, where CCAPI cannot be activated.
• Canon BLE — speaks Canon's own BR-E1 BLE protocol directly to a compatible Canon body. Wireless, no Pulsar hardware needed.

The app gives you precise control over exposures, intervals, bulb sequences, and complex multi-step flows on whichever transport you choose — they're mutually exclusive: connecting one disconnects the others.

1. Grant the permissions the app asks for on first launch (Bluetooth, Location, USB).
2. Open the Scan screen and pick how you want to connect:
 • Pulsar ESP32 module: power it on, tap its card under "Bluetooth devices".
 • Canon over Wi-Fi: enable CCAPI on the camera (one-time PC activation needed), join the camera's network, then tap its card under "Canon cameras".
 • Canon over USB-C: plug the cable in, accept the Android permission dialog, tap the camera under "USB cameras".
 • Canon BLE direct: put the camera in Bluetooth → Remote pair mode, tap its card under "Canon BLE remotes", confirm the Android pair dialog.
3. Once connected, the menu shows the shooting modes available for that transport.

Tip: the Scan screen has a "Camera setup help" button with body-specific instructions for the Canon paths. See the "Canon BLE in detail" section below for the full BR-E1 pairing walkthrough.

Four ways to drive the camera. Pick what fits your gear:

• Pulsar BLE (ESP32 module) — universal: any camera with a wired remote port. Lowest battery cost on the camera side. Firmware owns the run loop, so the phone can sleep mid-flow.
• CCAPI (Wi-Fi) — Canon EOS R-series with CCAPI activated. Adds live view, Star Focus, lens detection, and battery readout. Doubles camera battery drain because the body's Wi-Fi stays on; consider USB-C dummy-battery passthrough for long sessions.
• PTP (USB-C) — Canon EOS R / RP and most PTP cameras. Lowest latency (~10–30 ms per shot). Camera draws only ~5 %/h since Wi-Fi is off. Required for the EOS R, where CCAPI does not activate. Note: in PC-remote mode the body's mode dial locks until you disconnect.
• Canon BLE — speaks Canon's BR-E1 protocol directly. Wireless, no Pulsar hardware, no Wi-Fi setup. Every BR-E1-compatible body (EOS R/RP/R5/R6/Ra, 6D II, 77D, 200D, 800D, 850D, M50, M200, plus G7X III / G5X II). Bulb works via press-and-hold. No live view, lens info, or battery readout — those aren't in the BR-E1 protocol.

A "Simulator" entry on the Scan screen lets you exercise the UI and flows with no hardware connected.

Canon BLE direct lets you drive a Canon body wirelessly with no Pulsar hardware and no Wi-Fi setup. Pulsar speaks Canon's own BR-E1 remote-control protocol over Bluetooth Low Energy — the same protocol Canon's BR-E1 hardware remote uses.

Compatible bodies
• Every body on Canon's BR-E1 compatibility list: EOS R, RP, R5, R6, Ra, 6D Mark II, 77D, 800D (Rebel T7i), 200D (Rebel SL2), 850D, M50, M200, plus the PowerShot G7 X Mark III and G5 X Mark II.
• Bodies without BR-E1 support won't advertise the service and won't appear in the Canon BLE remotes section.

First-time pairing
• On the camera: enable Wireless communication → Bluetooth → set the mode to Remote, then choose Pair from the body's menu so it starts advertising.
• On the phone: open Pulsar's Scan screen. Your camera appears under "Canon BLE remotes". Tap its card.
• Android pops the system pair dialog; confirm the passkey matches the one shown on the camera. After this the bond lives in Android's OS keystore and the camera shows "Paired with: Pulsar" in its devices list.
• Subsequent connects skip the pair dialog and re-use the bond automatically.

What works
• Single-shot Timelapse (camera owns exposure).
• Bulb-style flows: Intervalometer with long exposures, Astro Mode, Dark Frame, Exposure Ramp. Pulsar holds the wireless shutter button down for the exposure duration, releases at the end — exactly like a physical BR-E1 would.
• Per-shot autofocus toggle: when on, Pulsar sends a brief half-press for AF lock before the full release.

What doesn't work
• Live view / Star Focus: the BR-E1 protocol has no live-view endpoint. Use CCAPI or USB-C PTP for Star Focus.
• Lens info auto-fill in Astro: not in the protocol. Type your focal length manually.
• Battery readout: not in the protocol. The status chip shows 0%.
• Programmatic settings (ISO / aperture / shutter speed): not in the protocol.

The mode-dial constraint
The protocol has no way to change the camera's mode dial or shutter-speed setting. For bulb-style flows you must set Bulb on the mode dial of the camera body yourself, and Manual exposure on the dial. For Timelapse the camera's shutter speed setting is the actual exposure time.

Auto-reconnect
If the camera sleeps or moves out of range, the connection drops and a reconnect banner appears. Wake the camera and Pulsar reconnects automatically. The bond survives app restarts — open Pulsar near a previously-paired camera and it will reconnect on its own.

Captures a series of photos at fixed intervals — ideal for time-lapses.

• Exposure: how long the shutter stays open each shot.
• Interval (gap): the pause between the end of one exposure and the start of the next.
• Shots: total number of photos to take (0 = unlimited).

The total cycle time per frame = exposure + interval.

On Canon transports (Wi-Fi or USB-C), if you set the exposure shorter than ~1 s the app fires single-shot captures and the camera owns the timing; longer exposures use bulb. Set Bulb on the body's mode dial for bulb runs.

Optimised for astrophotography. Uses the same intervalometer engine but adds sky-aware helpers.

• Maximum exposure is calculated from your focal length and sensor using the 500, 400, or NPF rule.
• On Canon transports, the focal length auto-fills from the attached lens when possible.
• Dashboard shows moon phase, twilight times, and Bortle-class estimation.
• Per-shot autofocus toggle on Canon transports (BLE-ESP captures don't expose AF separately).
• Pair with the Session Planner for multi-target night planning, and with Star Focus to nail focus first.

Gives you a simple shutter button on screen.

• HOLD: the shutter stays open as long as you press the button. Release to close.
• LOCK: tap once to open the shutter, tap again to close. Best for long exposures where you don't want to hold the button.
• Switch between Hold and Lock with the segmented buttons in the action area.

Great for testing your setup, one-off long exposures, or verifying the transport before kicking off a longer flow.

Captures calibration frames with the lens cap on, matching your light-frame exposure time.

• Dark frames record sensor noise so stacking software can subtract it.
• Set the same exposure as your light frames and cover the lens.
• Choose how many darks to capture — 20–30 is a common starting point.
• Built-in presets are provided based on common exposure lengths.

Ideally shoot darks at the end of a session so the sensor temperature matches your lights.

Gradually changes exposure time across a sequence — perfect for sunset-to-night holy-grail time-lapses.

• Set a start and end exposure plus the number of frames.
• The app smoothly ramps between the two values.
• Preview the ramp curve before starting.
• Combine with the Flows feature for multi-phase sequences.

Flows let you chain multiple shooting steps into a single automated sequence.

• Each step can be an Intervalometer, Astro, Dark Frames, Ramp, or Pause.
• Steps run in order — great for "shoot 100 lights, then 30 darks" workflows.
• Save your flows to the library and tag them for easy retrieval.
• Mark favourites so your most-used flows appear first.
• Built-in presets give you a quick starting point for common scenarios.
• The current step's mode and key parameters surface in the running-view chip so you always know what's firing.

A four-step guided wizard for nailing pinpoint focus on stars before kicking off an astro run. Available on the two Canon transports that support live view: CCAPI over Wi-Fi, and USB-C PTP on bodies that advertise the live-view op. Not available on Canon BLE direct — the BR-E1 protocol has no live-view endpoint.

• Prep: lens AF/MF switch to AF; mode dial to M (live view is disabled in Bulb).
• Aim: live view streams; tap a bright star to lock a small region of interest on it.
• Focus: a peak-luminance sharpness readout updates per frame; six drive-focus buttons («««, ««, «, », »», »»») step the motor — 1 = fine, 3 = coarse.
• Lock: live view auto-stops to save battery. Flip the lens to MF if it has the switch; for lenses without it, leave AF on — Pulsar already sends af=false on bulb runs.

Find it on the Tools tab once a Canon Wi-Fi or USB-C body is connected.

Uses the phone's compass + your GPS location + the current Polaris hour-angle to help align an equatorial mount.

• Hold the phone steady against the mount's polar axis (or use a hot-shoe / cold-shoe bracket).
• The on-screen reticle shows where Polaris should sit in the polar scope right now.
• Adjust the mount's altitude and azimuth knobs until your view matches.

Works offline — once the GPS fix is established you don't need a network.

An end-to-end diagnostic that fires shots across all available shooting modes against the currently connected transport (Pulsar BLE, CCAPI, USB-C PTP, or Canon BLE direct).

• When the transport supports bulb: 25 shots across all 5 wizards (Timelapse, Intervalometer-bulb, Astro, Dark Frame, Ramp).
• When the transport doesn't support bulb (some PowerShots over CCAPI, PTP bodies without the Canon RemoteRelease op): only the 5-shot Timelapse step runs and the bulb-based wizards are skipped automatically. The tile copy updates to reflect this.
• Useful after changing cables, switching bodies, pairing a Canon BLE body for the first time, or upgrading firmware — to confirm the active transport works end to end before committing to a real session.
• Find it on the Tools tab. Make sure the camera has space on the card and is set to Bulb on the dial where the test calls for it (Manual + Bulb on Canon bodies for the bulb-mode steps).

A live sky-conditions panel for astrophotographers.

• Moon phase and illumination percentage.
• Sunset, twilight (civil / nautical / astronomical), and sunrise times.
• Bortle-class estimate based on your GPS location.
• What's Up Tonight: a catalog of deep-sky objects currently above the horizon, sorted by altitude.

Plan a full night of imaging before you head out.

• Add multiple targets with individual exposure, interval, and frame-count settings.
• Reorder targets by dragging.
• See total session time and per-target estimates.
• Export the plan or load it directly into the Flows engine.
• Adjust default optics in Settings → Planner.

Every completed run gets a log entry: mode, exposure, interval, shot count, status (completed / stopped), and timestamps. Useful for reviewing what you actually shot vs what you planned.\n\nThe log survives uninstalls via the Backup & Restore export (Storage Access Framework — Google Drive, OneDrive, local storage, or any DocumentsProvider).

Fine-tune your Pulsar experience.

• Language: switch the app between English, Portuguese, Spanish, French, German, Japanese, and Chinese.
• Device: rename the Pulsar module, configure auto-off timer.
• GPIO Pins: remap shutter and focus pins if your cable wiring differs.
• Canon Wi-Fi cameras: saved bodies, per-camera nicknames, add-by-IP for when SSDP discovery is blocked. Credentials are stored encrypted at rest.
• Canon BLE pairing: handled by the OS — paired bodies live in Android's Bluetooth settings. To forget a Canon BLE camera, open Android Settings → Bluetooth, find the camera, tap "Forget". Pulsar remembers the last-paired MAC for auto-reconnect; tapping Disconnect in Pulsar clears that hint.
• Background activity: opt into Android's battery-optimisation exemption so long flows aren't suspended by Doze.
• Planner: default sensor and focal-length presets for the session planner.
• Backup / Restore: export or import your saved flows, presets, shot log, and settings as a JSON file via Android's Storage Access Framework.
• Updates: check for new firmware OTA or app updates.
• Device Info: hardware revision, firmware version, and BLE address.

• BLE range is typically 10–15 m in open air — keep the phone nearby. The same applies to Canon BLE direct: stay within ~10 m of the camera.
• For long Canon Wi-Fi sessions, use USB-C dummy-battery passthrough (e.g. DR-E18 on the EOS RP). CCAPI roughly halves a body's battery life.
• USB-C (PTP) is the most battery-efficient Canon transport — body draws ~5 %/h vs ~30 %/h on Wi-Fi. Canon BLE direct is also low-cost because the body's Wi-Fi radio stays off.
• In PC-remote mode (Canon over USB-C) the mode dial locks. To change Bulb/Manual on the body, disconnect first.
• Canon BLE has no way to change the mode dial remotely — set the body to Manual + Bulb yourself before starting a bulb flow.
• For Star Focus you need CCAPI (Wi-Fi) or USB-C PTP — Canon BLE has no live view. If you only have a Canon BLE connection, focus manually before the run.
• For astrophotography, arrive early and polar-align while twilight is fading. Use Star Focus before kicking off a long exposure run.
• Save your favourite workflows as Flows so you can start a session with one tap.
• Run Camera Test (Tools tab) after a hardware change or first pairing a new body to confirm the transport works end to end.
• Dark frames at end of session keep sensor temperature matched to your lights.

Pulsars were discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell as a graduate student in radio astronomy. This app borrows their name in humble tribute to her discovery and to her enduring championing of science.
Interval below 1 s — your camera may not have time to write the frame
Battery low (%1$d%%) — may not finish the sequence
